title: Open Science: Transparency, Reproducibility, and the Future of Research

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Korolev
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. I want to talk about something that is simultaneously a problem in science and a solution to it: data. The problem is that for most of science's modern history, the data underlying published findings were the private property of individual researchers and laboratories. The solution is what we now call "open science" — the movement to make data, materials, and methods available to any researcher who wants to verify, extend, or challenge a published finding.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Korolev
dialogue.text: Why does open data matter? Consider what happened during the replication crisis. Dozens of findings in psychology, medicine, and nutrition that had been widely accepted were found to be much weaker than believed, or not replicable at all. In several cases, when researchers attempted to recheck the original analysis, they couldn't — because the raw data no longer existed, had been lost, or was never shared. Without access to the original data, there is no way to identify whether a result was due to a genuine effect, a statistical error, or — in a small number of documented cases — deliberate fraud.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Korolev
dialogue.text: Open science has several components. Pre-registration is perhaps the most transformative. Before collecting any data, a researcher publicly registers their hypothesis, methodology, and analysis plan on a platform like the Open Science Framework. This makes it impossible to engage in "HARKing" — Hypothesising After the Results are Known — a practice in which researchers present exploratory findings as if they had been predicted in advance. Pre-registration creates a clear distinction between confirmatory research (testing a pre-specified hypothesis) and exploratory research (looking for patterns without a prior prediction).

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Korolev
dialogue.text: Open data means making the raw data from a study publicly available in a form that other researchers can access and analyse independently. This is increasingly required by major funding bodies and some journals. It makes fraud vastly harder to conceal, enables meta-analyses of pooled data from many studies, and allows researchers in under-resourced settings to conduct analyses without needing to run their own data collection.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Korolev
dialogue.text: Open methods — sharing detailed protocols, code, and materials — enables exact replication. If I replicate your study using your exact protocol and find a different result, that is much more informative than a conceptual replication using different materials. The more exactly the original conditions can be reproduced, the more clearly any discrepancy can be located and understood.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Korolev
dialogue.text: There are, of course, real challenges. Some data cannot be made publicly available for reasons of participant privacy — medical records, genetic data, data from vulnerable populations. Some researchers in competitive fields are reluctant to share data before they have exhausted their own analyses, fearing that rivals will publish using their data before they can. And in some scientific communities, there is simply no established culture of data sharing, making it harder for individual researchers to adopt open practices without institutional support.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Korolev
dialogue.text: But the direction of travel is clear. Funders, journals, and institutions are increasingly incentivising — and in some cases requiring — open practices. The long-term result will be a science that is more trustworthy, more efficient, and more equitable in its distribution of both data and credit. The question is not whether open science will become the norm, but how quickly.
